blocks.text: Gregor Mendel spent eight years crossing pea plants in a monastery garden and counting the offspring. He had never heard of a gene, never seen a chromosome, and had no microscope worth the name. Yet by careful counting alone he worked out the rules of inheritance that we still use today.

blocks.markdown:
## Mendel's two laws

**The law of segregation (first law).** The two alleles of a gene separate during the formation of gametes, so each gamete receives only one of them. This is a direct consequence of homologous chromosomes being pulled apart in meiosis I.

**The law of independent assortment (second law).** The alleles of one gene segregate independently of the alleles of another gene, provided the two genes are on different chromosomes. Which allele of the height gene a gamete receives has no bearing on which allele of the seed-colour gene it receives.

blocks.title: Monohybrid cross
blocks.text: A cross that follows the inheritance of a single characteristic controlled by one gene — for example height in peas. A dihybrid cross follows two characteristics at once.

blocks.markdown:
### Setting out a cross

There is a standard layout, and using it earns marks even when the arithmetic goes wrong.

1. State what each letter represents: let **T** = allele for tall, **t** = allele for dwarf, T dominant to t.
2. Write the **parental genotypes** and their phenotypes.
3. Write the **gametes** each parent can produce, circling or bracketing them.
4. Draw a **Punnett square** to combine every male gamete with every female gamete.
5. Read off the **genotypic ratio** and then the **phenotypic ratio**.

Always use the same letter in two cases for the two alleles of one gene.

blocks.title: Crossing two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt × Tt)
blocks.prompt: In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant to dwarf (t). Two heterozygous tall plants are crossed. Determine the genotypic and phenotypic ratios of the offspring.

steps.text: Define the symbols. Let T be the allele for tall and t the allele for dwarf, with T dominant to t.
Write the parents. Both are heterozygous tall, so both have the genotype Tt.
Work out the gametes. By the law of segregation each Tt parent produces two kinds of gamete in equal numbers: T and t.
Combine them in a Punnett square. Placing the father's gametes across the top and the mother's down the side gives four equally likely combinations: TT, Tt, Tt and tt.
Read the genotypic ratio: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt.
Convert to phenotypes. TT and Tt are both tall because T is dominant, so three of the four are tall and one is dwarf. The phenotypic ratio is 3 tall : 1 dwarf, which is the classic Mendelian ratio.

blocks.answer: Genotypic ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. Phenotypic ratio 3 tall : 1 dwarf, so 75% of the offspring are expected to be tall.

blocks.caption: Three of the four boxes give a tall plant, hence the 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio

blocks.markdown:
### The test cross

A tall pea plant may be TT or Tt, and you cannot tell by looking. To find out, cross it with a **homozygous recessive** plant (tt) — this is the **test cross** or back cross.

If the unknown is **TT**, every gamete carries T, so every offspring is Tt and **all** are tall.

If the unknown is **Tt**, half its gametes carry t. Crossed with tt, the offspring are 1 Tt : 1 tt, so **half are dwarf**.

So a single dwarf offspring proves the parent was heterozygous.

blocks.caption: The five possible monohybrid crosses. Memorising these ratios makes most questions immediate.

blocks.markdown:
### When dominance is not complete

In some organisms the heterozygote shows a phenotype in between the two homozygotes. In *Mirabilis jalapa*, the four o'clock plant, a red-flowered plant (RR) crossed with a white-flowered plant (rr) gives **all pink** offspring (Rr). Crossing two pink plants then gives 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white — a phenotypic ratio of 1 : 2 : 1 rather than 3 : 1, because each genotype now has its own appearance. This is **incomplete dominance**.

blocks.title: Ratios are probabilities, not guarantees
blocks.text: A 3 : 1 ratio means each offspring has a 3 in 4 chance of being tall. In a family of four, all four could be tall — just as four tosses of a coin can all be heads. Ratios only approach the predicted values in large numbers of offspring, which is why Mendel counted thousands of plants.

blocks.title: Always show the working
blocks.text: Marks are awarded for defining the symbols, stating the parental genotypes, showing the gametes and drawing the Punnett square — not only for the final ratio. A bare answer of '3 : 1' typically scores one mark out of five.

points: The law of segregation states that the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation.
The law of independent assortment states that genes on different chromosomes are inherited independently of each other.
A Tt × Tt cross gives a genotypic ratio of 1 : 2 : 1 and a phenotypic ratio of 3 : 1.
A test cross with a homozygous recessive individual reveals whether an organism showing the dominant phenotype is homozygous or heterozygous.
Under incomplete dominance the heterozygote is intermediate, so a self-cross gives a 1 : 2 : 1 phenotypic ratio.
